resources.string: The look of the whole launcher: Classic is the flat Windows Phone look, Modern Glass is frosted glass, Modern Droid follows Material You. It changes surfaces, buttons and animations, not your tiles.
Dark, light, as the phone says, or by the hour (or sunrise and sunset). Dark with an OLED screen also saves battery.
The hours of the dark theme when the theme follows the hour. The end may be earlier than the start: the night goes through midnight.
Pure black backgrounds in the dark theme: on an OLED screen those pixels are off, so more contrast and less battery. No effect in the light theme or on an LCD screen.
Builds the theme from the colors of your Android wallpaper (Android 12 and later). Off, the theme uses the accent you choose below.
The color of live tiles, buttons and highlights: one of the 21 Windows Phone colors, or your own with three sliders.
A second accent color used only while the dark theme is on, for example a softer one at night.
The accent follows the Start photo: the closest of the 21 Windows Phone colors to its main color. It needs a photo; choosing a color by hand stops it.
A photo behind Start, chosen from your gallery. The tiles of the built-in apps show it through them. The photo stays on the phone.
While MetroWin is your home app, Android’s wallpaper is the Start photo (or its color), which is what the recent-apps screen shows behind the cards. Off, Android keeps its own wallpaper.
Each Start screen can have its own photo. A screen without one shows the photo chosen for all.
How the Start photo is placed: filled, fitted, stretched, tiled or centered, and which part of it stays in view when you zoom in.
Chooses which parts of the launcher use the accent color. Where a part is off, it uses a grey that suits the theme.
Gives a mini app a color of its own. “Like the theme” makes it follow the accent above.
How much of the Start photo shows through the tiles: more transparent tiles show more photo and less color.
Every tile becomes a window onto the photo, with no gap between tiles, as on Windows Phone. It needs a Start photo.
The photo moves slower than the tiles when you scroll, for a feeling of depth. It needs a Start photo and is off with reduced motion.

The photo behind the tiles moves by this share of the speed of the tiles when you scroll. Still keeps it in place and the tiles slide over it; the more you give it, the closer it follows them. It needs a Start photo and the parallax above.
A big title (start, apps) behind the pages, which moves slower than the page when it slides, as in the Windows Phone panorama.
The headings of the sections of the hubs (Photos, People, News) as large as in Windows Phone, 49.5 dp instead of 27. Only in the Classic look.

A theme file holds the colors, dark or light mode, clock, tile size and icon pack, not your tiles. Export it to keep or share the look; import one to apply it. Your tiles and other settings do not change.
Lets the launcher follow the rotation of the phone, or keeps it upright (portrait) or sideways (landscape).
How an app opens from a tile: the original Windows Phone turnstile, a softer modern one, expanding out of the tile, fade, slide, rise, zoom or nothing. With reduced motion apps open at once.
How much room Start, the app list and the pages leave at the sides. Compact gives tiles and text a little more width, wide a little less. It never gets so extreme that pages are hard to use.
The language of the launcher itself, apart from the phone’s language (Android 13 and later). The first choice follows the language of the phone.

Asks the screen for its fastest mode (120 Hz and more) only while you use the phone; three seconds after the last touch it goes back to 60 Hz. A smoother feel at a small battery cost; off lets Android decide.
Makes the tiles smaller so more of them fit across. Only the layout changes; your tiles stay.
How many small tiles fit across Start. Automatic follows your screen; a number is limited so tiles never get too small to touch.
A tile stays where you drop it, on any cell, and the others do not move up to fill the gap. Off, the tiles flow in order again; nothing you placed is lost.
Shows the name of the app under its tile. Off, the tiles are only their pictures.
The space between tiles, from narrow to wide.
How many Start screens you have (one to three). More screens mean swiping sideways; tiles you remove from a screen stay on it until you move them.
The Start screen the launcher returns to when you press Home or come back from another app.
Where the other Start screens are, seen from the one the launcher opens on. To the left, the app list stays to the right of everything.
Puts the app list to the left of Start instead of the right: swipe right from Start to reach it. The dots, the big titles and the edge swipe follow.
What leads to the app list after the last tile: the round arrow, three plain dots, or nothing for a cleaner screen. Swiping works either way.
Offers the Large size (four tiles across and four down) in the edit bar and the resize arrow. Tiles that are already large stay large.
On a wide screen (a tablet, a big window) shows Start and the app list side by side instead of one swipe away. A phone, even on its side, keeps the pages.
Shows the titles written above groups of tiles and starts each group on its own row. Off, Start is one plain grid; the titles are kept.
Offers the collage style (many small pictures side by side) to tiles that show photos.
A wide Calendar tile lists the next events; a large one shows the month and the next events. It reads the calendar on the phone and needs its permission.
The Battery tile says how long the charge should last, as Android predicts it (Android 12 and later).
Previous, play or pause and next on the Music tile while something plays. They need notification access, to find the player.
Save the Start screens as they are now under a name (home, work, travel), then put one back with a touch or update it. A layout does not change your settings, only the tiles.
Gives a layout an hour: at that hour it takes Start over, once. A layout you choose by hand stays until the next hour comes.
Puts back the tiles Start had when you installed the launcher and takes away the ones you added (contacts, sites, notes, widgets). It asks twice, and Undo brings back everything but the widgets.
Shows the time and the date above the tiles of Start.
The clock in 12 or 24 hours, or as the phone says.
An extra line under the date of the clock of Start. It works only while the clock of Start is on.
A second clock under the date, for another city or time zone (a relative abroad, a colleague).
A touch on the time opens the clock app, on the date the calendar. Off, the clock of Start is only to look at.
The bar at the bottom while you edit the tiles: with the … button its buttons show their names.

The look of the bar of actions that appears while you edit: the modern one or the retro one of Windows Phone (the “super” bar). “Retro, minimized” keeps only a thin strip with the … until you touch it.
The goal the Steps tile counts toward. It reads the step counter of the phone and needs the activity permission; off shows no goal.
When you come back from another app after this long, Start is at the top, as after Home. Off, Start stays where you left it.
Tiles cannot be moved, resized, removed or added by mistake. Switch it off here to change them again.
The clock and the tiles begin lower on the screen, within reach of the thumb on a big phone. Scroll to see the rest.
How many changes to Start the launcher remembers, to undo them one by one. More steps use a little more space.
Takes back the last change to Start (a moved, resized, removed or added tile). It is grey when there is nothing to undo.
Every minute everything moves by a few pixels, slowly, so that what stays the same for hours does not burn into an OLED screen. The navigation buttons follow. Useful only on OLED.
Shows the lock screen now, as it would look when the screen comes on, so you can try your choices.

When the screen is off, the Metro lock screen is made ready over Android’s one and is there when the screen comes on; swipe up to reach Android’s. It needs the accessibility service and is not shown during a call.
A photo only for the lock screen. Without it the lock screen uses the Start photo, and black if there is none.
A line of the lock screen. Anyone who looks at the screen can read it; turn it off if you prefer not to show it.
The weather the Weather tile fetched last. The lock screen itself fetches nothing.
The next event of your calendar in the next 24 hours. It needs the calendar permission, and anyone who sees the screen can read it.
Sets the photo (or black) as the wallpaper of Android’s own lock screen, so the two match.

Android does not let a launcher replace its lock screen, so the Metro lock screen also runs as the screen saver: choose “Metro lock screen” in Android’s screen saver settings and it shows while the phone charges or rests on a dock. Swipe up to leave.
Up to five apps with the number of their notifications, under the time. Without a choice, the apps with the most notifications. It needs notification access.
Writes out the last notification of an app (who and what) on the lock screen. Anyone who sees the screen reads it: use it only for apps you do not mind showing.
Leaves a spot for your finger so Android reads it through the picture. Turn it off if the sensor is on the side or the back of the phone.
The height of the fingerprint spot on the screen, to match where your phone’s sensor is.
Hides Android’s fingerprint icon under the MetroWin one. On some phones the sensor then stops reading: if your finger no longer unlocks, turn this off.
The apps with news on the lock screen stay in one row: icons shrink to fit, and +N says how many did not fit. Off: larger icons on more rows.
While a song plays, shows its cover, its name and the buttons to skip and pause. It needs notification access to find the player.

Hides the status bar for more room on Start. A swipe from the top edge shows it for a moment; with the bar hidden that swipe is Android’s, so open the Action Center with a gesture from the Gestures page.
Draws the Windows Phone status bar in place of Android’s: notifications on the left, and on the right signal, Wi-Fi, battery with its percentage and time. It also takes Android’s bar out of the way.

Draws the bar over the status bar of Android in apps outside the launcher. It covers the top of the app and takes no touch. It needs the screen lock service (accessibility); banking apps are left alone in safe mode.

Draws the Windows Phone status bar inside the mini apps (Calculator, Notes, Mail…), with the pages starting under it. It needs the Windows Phone status bar to be on, and it steps aside when the bar over other apps is on.
A short banner when the cable goes in, and the battery filling in the status bar and on the lock screen while it charges. With reduced motion only the state stays.
Shows or hides this icon in the MetroWin status bar. It only changes the bar; the phone’s own state does not change.
Shows the kind of network (5G, 4G, 3G, E) next to the signal. Android tells it only to apps that may read the phone state, so turning it on asks for that permission.

With two SIMs, chooses which one the status bar shows as the main one (the big signal bars and the kind of network); the other goes under it, smaller. By default the phone’s own choice. With one SIM it changes nothing.
The shape of the icons of apps on tiles and in the list: as they come, round, square or squircle.
An app tile takes the main color of its icon instead of the accent. Grey icons keep the accent.
Icons of every app turn to translucent glass and their tiles see through, so a Start background shows behind them. Built-in apps keep their Metro glyph.
The icon of an app fills its tile, as the pictures of the tiles did on Windows Phone, instead of sitting small in the middle. Built-in apps keep their Metro glyph.
A pack replaces the icons of the apps it has an icon for. The Metro apps of the phone keep their glyphs. You can still choose the icon of one app apart (see “icons per app”).
Opens the Play Store search for icon packs (or its web page). Packs you install appear in the list above. The launcher sends nothing.
Choose the icon of one app on its own: from an icon pack, or the original. It works with the packs you have installed.
Makes the text of the whole launcher smaller or bigger, from 85% to 130%. The pages never break: very large text is capped.
Makes all the text of the launcher heavier. Android’s bold text setting turns it on too.
The font of the launcher: twenty come with it, you can bring your own (.ttf or .otf), or use the font of the phone, which comes first when on. The file is copied into the launcher and not shared.
Screens fade instead of swinging, tiles stop flipping and tilting, and apps open without an animation. It is also on whenever Android has animations removed. It saves a little battery.
Tiles get a white frame and stay solid over a Start photo, and grey text turns to full color. Easier to read in sunlight or with low vision.

Every tile says what it is and its notifications. In the TalkBack actions menu a tile offers unpin, change size, move earlier or later (folders: rename, take apart). The app list reads each app and offers its menu.
Chooses what this gesture does: lock the screen, torch, voice, search, open an app and more. With the Action Center off, its action is not offered. Locking the screen uses the accessibility service.
Adds a Recent apps tile to Android’s quick settings (Android 13 and later), so you can open the recent apps from the Android panel too.

Android lets an app lock the screen, open the recent apps or draw over other apps only through an accessibility service. This one reads nothing from the screen; it only learns which app is in front. You turn it on in Android’s accessibility settings.
A pull down from the top edge opens the Action Center from any page, not only from the top of Start.
Two fingers swiping up or down together close a mini app and go back to Start. Off by default: a pinch on a photo can drift into it.
A double tap on an empty spot of the apps list turns the screen off, and on Start too when the double tap above does nothing. Off by default. It needs the accessibility service.
On Start, the swipe from the edge that Android uses for Back goes to the next or previous page instead.
A click sound or a short buzz when you touch something. Off by default. The buzz follows the strength set below.
How fast the animations run: 100% is as designed, 200% twice as fast. Springs (the bounce of a tile) keep their own pace.
How far a tile or a button leans away from the finger when pressed. 0% keeps only the sinking. It is the press of the Classic look.
The strength of the vibration of a tap (when “vibrate on tap” is on): 0% is none, 200% twice the usual.
How loud the click of a tap and the little Metro sounds are while the launcher is on screen, as a share of the phone’s volume: 0% is silent. Sounds heard over other apps keep the phone’s volume.

Draws back, the Windows logo and search over Android’s buttons. A long press on the logo opens the recent apps. It needs the accessibility service and Android’s three-button navigation; with gesture navigation it has nothing to draw over.

While a game is in front, the Windows Phone status bar and navigation buttons slide away so they do not cover it. Swipe up from the bottom edge for the buttons, down from the top edge for the status bar. It needs the accessibility service.
The games the phone knows are listed. A game that is not recognized (the bars stay over it): search for it and switch it on. A wrong one: switch it off.
How far apart back, the Windows logo and search are in the navigation bar, from 50 to 110 percent of the usual distance.
How long the Windows logo is held to open the recent apps, from 0.3 to 1.5 seconds. They open as the time is up, without lifting the finger.

Off, the panel with notifications and quick buttons is gone (in the launcher and over other apps), the gestures that opened it do nothing, and notifications stay in Android’s own shade with their own sounds. Calls, alarms and music are never touched.
A swipe down from the very top edge (a thin 20 dp strip) opens the Action Center over the app you are in. It needs the accessibility service, the only kind of window that can sit over the status bar.

The four quick buttons on top of the Action Center. Pick a slot, then the action; hold and drag to reorder. The torch really switches on; the others open the right screen of Android (or work directly with Shizuku).

For advanced users. Shizuku lets some buttons (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and others) switch on the spot instead of opening Android’s screen. How to turn Shizuku on is in the Shizuku Terminal app; this only leads there.
The flashlight lit from the Action Center or from Start goes out by itself after this time (an Android alarm, so it may be a little late). It saves battery if you forget it.
Buttons under the sound modes: a touch sets the ringtone, media and alarm volumes to those of the preset. Save the volumes the phone has now as a preset with a name.

Two sliders and the sound, vibration and silent buttons in the Action Center. The volume needs no permission; the brightness needs the “modify system settings” access, which you give in an Android screen.
The volume keys draw a Metro panel over the launcher for what is sounding now: the call, the music (with the app’s name) or the ringer. It follows the real volume of the phone.

The permission that lets the launcher read notifications. It is given in an Android screen, and it is what live tiles, the Action Center and the lock screen counters need. The launcher keeps what it reads on the phone and sends nothing.

The tile of an app turns over to show what its notifications say: messages, pictures, the song that plays. Anyone who sees your screen sees it too, so it is off until you turn it on. Choose what shows in the live tiles page.
Shows a “reply” link on messages that can be answered, and sends your answer to the app that posted them. It needs notification access and the Action Center on.
An app with several notifications shows as one line you can open. Swiping it away clears them all.
A Metro banner at the top while the launcher is on screen. Android’s own banner may show too: turn it off for an app in that app’s notification settings.

The same banner over the app you are in, when the launcher is not on screen. Not on the lock screen, not for silent notifications, not when Do Not Disturb blocks them. It needs the permission to draw over other apps.
A long press on a notification offers to silence its app for an hour, eight hours or until morning: its notifications and banners stay out of sight and come back when the time is up.

Opening an app from Start or the app list takes away its notifications and the number on its tile. They stay in the history of the Action Center for a while. Opening it from elsewhere (its notification, the recent apps) does not.
In the Action Center, messages and calls come before the other notifications.

A notification with one of your words is taken away from Android and shown nowhere: not in the Action Center, not as a banner, not on the lock screen. Calls, alarms and music are never touched. Careful with short words.
How long the timed quiet mode of the Action Center lasts when you start it, from 15 minutes to 4 hours.
The glide heard when the Action Center comes down and goes back up. It needs the Metro sounds.
A chime for a new notification and a short glide when the Action Center comes down or goes, also over other apps. They follow the volume of the phone.

Every notification that arrives goes from Android’s shade to the Action Center: also the quiet ones, those that come with the screen off, and those already there. Calls, alarms, music and anything ongoing stay where they are. It needs the banner on.
Choose for each app where its notifications show: the Action Center, the lock screen, the banner. The sound and vibration belong to Android: the notification page of each app opens from here.

Chooses when the launcher saves battery: automatic (when Android’s battery saver is on, or the battery is at 20% or less and not charging), always, or never. Saving means the tiles stop flipping and the screen is not asked for its fastest refresh rate.
A microphone at the top of Start starts the voice assistant with one touch, as the gesture does.
Shows a microphone in the search box of the app list. It needs the microphone permission the first time you use it.
Uses the offline voice model when the phone has one for your language, so nothing leaves the phone. Otherwise your voice goes to the speech service you chose in Android.

“Call Anna” places the call without opening the dialer first. Off, the dialer opens with the number written in, one tap from calling, so a word heard wrong does not call anyone. Android asks for the phone permission the first time.
Starts listening now, so you can test your microphone and the recognition before using it for real.
The apps you open most from the launcher, in a group at the top of the list. The counts stay on this phone and are not part of the backups.
The apps installed in the last week, at the top of the list. Right after setting up or restoring a phone nothing is called new.
Adds a group “recent” at the top of the list with the apps you opened last. The list stays kept on this phone and is not part of the backups. Off by default.
Smaller squares and tighter rows in the app list: more apps on the screen.
Chips under the search box that show only the apps of one kind. Only the apps that say what they are (games, social, music…) appear in them.
Apps you hid from the list. Touch one to show it again. Hidden apps still open from their tile on Start.
Apps you gave another name. Touch one to give it back its own name.

Apps that ask for your fingerprint or screen lock before opening from the launcher (list, tiles, search, voice). Touch one to stop asking. The app can still be opened from a notification, the recent apps or another app: this is a lock for the launcher, not for Android.

While a bank, card or wallet app is in front, the launcher takes every window of its own away (buttons, status bar over apps, banners, the Action Center strip) and puts them back when you leave, because banks refuse to run under overlays. Banks are found by name; add or remove apps below.
The search box also looks in your contacts. It needs the contacts permission, read on the phone only while you search.
The search box also finds the settings of Android (Wi-Fi, display, battery…) and opens the right screen.
Finds the settings of the launcher by name or by what they are for, and opens the page where each one is. It is the same search as at the top of these settings.
Also looks in the notes and the things to do of the launcher. Locked notes and the bin are left out.
Looks in the words of notes and lists, countdowns, counters and the names of sites pinned to Start.
Offers a web search for what you typed, with the engine chosen below. The browser opens only when you touch it.
The web search engine: DuckDuckGo, Google, Bing, Brave, Ecosia, Startpage or Qwant, or the browser’s own.
Sums (12*3+4, 15% of 80), conversions (5 km in miles), phone numbers, links, e-mail addresses, and timers and alarms (“timer 10 minutes”), all worked out on the phone.
Type torch, silent, vibrate, wifi, bluetooth… and the first result does it, as the Action Center button would.
A different hint about the launcher each day, in the Today card of the app list (it needs the Today card).

Reminders, events (Google Calendar), notes (Google Keep), places near you (Google Maps), codes and text (Google Lens): “remind me to call Anna tomorrow at 6”, “pharmacy near me”. It hands the request to the app that does it.
Digits find contacts by the letters on the keys (266 finds Ann) and by their number, as on old phones with a keypad.
A card above the search box with the date, the next event, the weather and the reminders. What it shows is chosen by the switches that follow.
A line of the Today card in the app list. Off, the line is left out. It works only while the Today card is on.
“100 usd in eur”, “50 dollars in euros”. It asks api.frankfurter.dev (the rates of the European Central Bank) once in a while and sends nothing you type. Off until you turn it on.
Also looks in the notifications that wait in the Action Center. They are read on the phone, only while you search.
A word and a colon in front narrow the search: app:, contact:, setting:, file:, event:, notif:, tile:, web: (or a:, c:, s:, f:, e:, n:, t:, w:).
Looks in your files by name: documents, photos, videos, music. Choose the kinds. It reads names on the phone only while you search and needs the matching permission.
Events of the next six months whose title matches. It needs the calendar permission; it is read on the phone and nothing leaves it.
The last searches are offered when you touch the search box. They stay on this phone and are not part of the backups.
Deletes the recent searches now. It cannot be undone.

The city of the Weather tile: by name, or with your location (it asks for the location permission). You can follow more cities. The forecast comes from Open-Meteo over the internet; nothing else leaves the phone.
Shows temperatures in Fahrenheit instead of Celsius.
Where the Photos tile takes its pictures from (all, an album, or photos you choose) and which gallery app it opens. It needs the photos permission; the pictures are not copied or sent anywhere.
The same switch as in the notifications page: the tile of an app turns over to show what its notifications say. It puts the text of your messages on Start, so it stays off until you turn it on.
Android asks for it in its own screen. The launcher only reads the notifications that are already up, and keeps them on the phone.
A face for each chat, with who wrote, the last line and the picture of the sender; other notifications (a like, a reply) as a title and a line. The counter adds up the messages one by one.
Shows only who wrote or which app it is from: the text of messages and notifications stays off the tiles, for anyone who sees your screen.
One kind of live content on the tiles (pictures, the song that plays, downloads and progress), read from notifications. Turn it off to keep it off the tiles.
Switch an app off and its tile stays as it is. An app appears here once it has something to show.
If an app shows nothing on its tile, look here: if it is listed, the tile can show it; if not, the app wrote nothing the launcher can read.
One block of the weather tile and of its page (now, hourly, daily, wind…). Turn it off to leave it out.
Shows the apps of that profile in the app list and the search, or hides them from the launcher. It hides them only here: Android still has them.

Choose any folder, also one of Google Drive or another cloud app that shows in the file picker. The layout is saved there as metrowin-layout.json when the launcher goes to the background, no more often than you choose. What you save goes where you choose, not to any server of the launcher.
Each backup is also kept under the minute it was made, and the oldest ones go once there are more than this number. Touch one below to put it back.

Saves the list of the apps installed on this phone to a file, or reads one: after a change of phone it shows the apps the new one does not have yet, with a link to the store. The apps themselves are not saved.
Sends the layout as a file through the share sheet of Android (mail, chat, cloud). It goes only where you send it.
Back up now saves a copy to the folder at once; restore puts one back (you choose which parts: Start, settings, look, data); stop using this folder only forgets the folder, your files in it stay.

Keeps Start in sync between your phones through the backup folder: the layout is written as an encrypted file and the other phone reads it. It needs the same passphrase on every phone. If two phones changed at once, the copy of the other is kept for you to put back.

Use the same passphrase on every phone. The file is encrypted with it (AES-256) before it goes in the folder. It stays on this phone and is never written to the folder: if you lose it, the synced data cannot be read.
Syncs at once instead of waiting for the next time the launcher goes to the background.
Saves the Start screens, the shortcuts and the settings in a file you can keep or copy to another phone. Nothing goes anywhere else.
Replaces the Start screens and the settings with those of a file. Apps this phone does not have are left out. You choose which parts to put back before anything changes.
The apps the child can open. Only these appear in the kid’s corner; all the others stay out of reach.
Write what went wrong and what you were doing. The more precise, the easier it is to find. Nothing is sent until you send the mail yourself.
Opens your mail app with the address, the subject and the log of the launcher already attached. You read it and send it; the log can show app names, so check it.
The version and build number of the launcher: useful to say which one you have when you ask for help or report a problem.
Checks GitHub for a newer release when you ask and, if there is one, downloads and installs it after your touch. Nothing is installed without it. The check sends nothing about you.
Asks GitHub for the latest release every 12 hours when there is a connection, and tells you with a notification. Nothing is installed without your touch.
Model, Android, memory, space and how long the phone has been on, shown on this page. Nothing leaves the phone.
The tour of the launcher, page by page, with a link to the settings of each feature and the permissions it can ask for, one at a time.
The people and the free software this launcher is built on, with their licenses.
Other apps by the same author. Touch a picture to enlarge it. Free ones have open source, no ads and no trackers; the others do not publish their code.
Starts a Start screen with only the apps you chose, for a child: the rest of the phone stays out of reach. To leave, you confirm with your screen lock, so a child cannot go back to the normal Start.

Pauses the work profile or the private space: a paused profile runs nothing and its apps cannot be opened until you resume it. Your data stays. Android asks for your authentication to unlock the private space.

The Finance tile: the currency its values are shown in, and up to four things to follow. Currencies come from the European Central Bank (api.frankfurter.dev), coins from CoinGecko; there are no stock prices. Only the rates are fetched, nothing you own is sent.

How a tile changes face: flip (the tile turns over), slide (the new face slides in from below) or mixed (each tile in its own way). Nothing moves by itself while saving battery or with reduced motion.

An app that asks for the permission can put a title, a line of text and a number on its own tile, like a Windows Phone live tile: only its own tile, the launcher knows who is asking. Each app that does appears in a list where you can clear what it published.
How often the launcher saves a copy to the folder by itself: every day, week or month; never means you save by hand with “back up now”. It runs when the launcher goes to the background.

How the whole launcher looks: dark or light theme, the accent color, the photo behind Start, the style (classic, glass, droid), and the screen: rotation, how apps open, refresh rate and language. Theme files let you save the look and share it. Nothing here costs battery, except a very high refresh rate.

Your Start screen: how many tiles per row, how many Start screens, names and spacing, saved layouts, the clock and date on top, live tiles (weather, photos, messages) and how Start behaves (back to the top, lock layout, undo). Live tiles read data from your phone only when you allow it.

The Metro lock screen of the launcher: its photo, what it shows (clock, alarm, notifications, weather, next event, music), the fingerprint icon and the screensaver while charging. It does not replace your PIN or fingerprint: the security of the phone stays Android’s.

The bars around your apps. The MetroWin status bar (signal, clock, battery; it can also sit over other apps), the Action Center you pull down from the top (quick buttons, sliders, volume panel) and the navigation bar with the three Windows Phone buttons. Showing a bar over other apps needs the accessibility service, which the launcher uses only to draw it.

What your fingers can do: double tap and two-finger swipes on Start, pulls from the edges, the Recent apps tile, and how a touch feels (sound, vibration, animation speed). The voice page lets you speak to the launcher. Some gestures use the accessibility service, only to lock the screen or draw over other apps.

Your apps: what the app list shows at the top, hidden and renamed apps, icon packs and the icon of a single app, and the search box (what it looks in, what it answers, which web engine it uses). Searching in contacts, calendar or files asks for the matching permission only when you turn it on.

The mini apps built into the launcher (Messages, Mail, Calendar, Calculator, Notes and the others) have their own switches here, the same ones as in the options menu of each app. A change applies the next time the app is opened. The accent color of the mini apps is on the Look page.

How notifications reach you: the permission to read them, the banner over other apps, replies from the panel, grouping, sounds, filtering by words, timed quiet mode and choices for each app. Reading notifications needs notification access; the launcher keeps what it reads on the phone and does not send it anywhere.

What keeps your things safe: the safe mode for banking apps (the launcher takes its own windows away while one is open, because banks refuse to run under overlays), apps locked behind your fingerprint, and the kid’s corner, a Start with only the apps you choose.

How much the launcher uses the battery. Power saving makes it do less when the battery is low. Off screen, or with another app in front, the launcher runs no timers and reads nothing. Excluding it from Android’s battery optimization keeps notifications and sync alive.

Make the launcher easier to read and use: bigger or bolder text, a font of your own, fewer animations, stronger contrast, and the use of TalkBack. These apply to the whole launcher and to the mini apps. Text size is limited so that the pages never break.

Keeping your setup safe: save the layout and settings to a file or to a folder (with automatic copies), restore them, share them, sync two phones with an encrypted file in a folder you choose, and pause or hide the work profile and the private space. Nothing is sent to any server: you choose the folder.

The version of the launcher and the update from GitHub (checked only when you ask, or every 12 hours if you turn it on), information about the phone, the tutorial to see again, a bug report with the log of the app, the credits and the other projects of the author.

FOLDERS
folders and groups
Keep Start tidy without losing anything: put tiles together in a folder, or lay small tiles side by side as a group.
Drop a tile on the middle of another one to make a folder. A folder opens in place, over Start.
Touch and hold a tile, touch the folder button and pick several tiles at once. In the app list, “add to folder” does the same.
Make a tile small and drag other small tiles to the empty squares beside it: that is a group, without a folder. A group can have a title, shown or hidden in the settings.
SCREENS AND LAYOUTS
screens and layouts
You can have up to three Start screens, and keep the way Start is arranged under a name.
Choose how many Start screens you have, which one the launcher returns to, and where the others are.
Save Start as it is now as a layout (home, work, travel), put one back with a touch, or give it an hour so it takes over by itself.
Moved something by mistake? Undo brings back the last changes. “Lock the layout” stops tiles from being moved at all, and “Start lower down” brings everything within reach of your thumb.
INFO TILE
the info tile
One tile that shows what you look at most, turning from one thing to the next: the time, your next event, the next alarm, your photos, the battery or the weather.
Add it to Start like any other tile. You can add more than one: a clock tile and a weather tile, for example.
Its choices let you pick the faces it turns through, how fast it turns, a second time zone and the album the photos come from.
“Smart order” puts first what matters now: at night only the time, and an event or an alarm within the hour stays alone. A switch makes it show only the time while saving battery.
A touch opens what the face on show is about: the calendar, the alarms, the photos or the battery.
SEARCH
search and answers
The box of the app list finds almost everything on the phone, and answers while you type.

It looks in apps (by name, by initials such as gm for Google Maps, even with typos), contacts, calendar events, files, notes, what is on Start, notifications, Android settings and these settings. You choose which ones.
Quick answers: sums, unit and currency conversions, timers and alarms (“timer 10 minutes”), dice. A smart dial finds contacts from digits.
A word and a colon narrow the search: app:, contact:, setting:, file:, event:, notif:, tile:, web:. The enter key of the keyboard opens the first result.
The Today card above the box shows the date, the next event, the weather and your reminders. The web search uses the engine you choose.
ICONS
icons and icon packs
Change the icon of every app, or of one app only.
Choose the shape of the icons, let a tile take its color from its icon, or turn the icons to glass or let them fill the tile.
Install icon packs from the Play Store (Nova, ADW, Apex, Smart and others) and pick one: it replaces the icons it has.
For a single app you can pick an icon from any installed pack, or go back to the original, without changing the others.
VOICE
talk to your phone
Say it instead of typing: the launcher understands a few commands, in English and Italian.
Tap the microphone in the search box, or turn on the assistant icon on Start. Try “open Maps” or “call Anna”.
It can open an app, call someone, set a timer or an alarm, switch on the torch, search, tell the weather and more.

When the phone has your language offline, the voice is recognized on the phone and goes nowhere; otherwise it goes to the speech service chosen in Android. “Call” can dial at once or open the dialer with the number written in.
MINI APPS
apps inside the launcher
MetroWin comes with its own small apps in the Windows Phone style: no ads, and nothing is sent anywhere.
Phone, Messages, Mail, Calendar, People, Photos, Music, Files, Notes, To do, Calculator, Recorder, Wallet, News, Data Sense, Terminal and more. Find them in the app list or pin them to Start.
They open and close with the same animations and sounds as Start. Two fingers swiping together can take you back to Start (it is off until you turn it on).
Each one has an options menu inside; the same switches are all together in the settings, where the search finds them. Each app can also have an accent color of its own.
PHONE
calls and two SIMs
The Phone app has a keypad and a call screen in the Windows Phone style, and uses the contacts of People.
With two SIMs, a call or a text asks which SIM to use. You can set a default SIM for calls and another for texts, and keep a SIM for a contact so it is never asked again.
Phone opens on the keypad: a long press on 1 calls the voicemail, and 2 to 9 can be speed dials. The call log is grouped, with a card and a note for each number.
The tile counts only the missed calls you have not seen yet. During a call you can use the speakerphone and choose Bluetooth as the audio route.
NOTIFICATIONS
your notifications
The Action Center collects the notifications of every app; you decide what it does with them.
Reply from the panel when the app allows it, group the notifications of an app, put messages and calls first, and silence an app for an hour, eight hours or until morning.
Leave out the notifications that contain words you list: they are shown nowhere. Calls, alarms and music are never touched.
A Metro banner can show at the top, also over other apps, with the chimes and glides of Windows Phone. For each app you choose where its notifications show.
The launcher reads notifications only to show them to you, and keeps what it reads on the phone. Opening an app from Start clears its notifications and the number on its tile.
BARS
status bar and buttons
The status bar and the three buttons of Windows Phone can take the place of Android’s.
The MetroWin status bar shows notifications at the left and signal, Wi-Fi, battery and time at the right. Each icon can be turned off, and the bar can sit over other apps too.
The navigation bar draws back, the Windows logo and search over the three buttons of Android. Hold the logo to open the recent apps, and choose how far apart the buttons are.
In games and videos the bars slide away so they do not cover the picture; one thin swipe from the edge brings them back. You can add a game the launcher does not know.
Drawing over other apps uses the accessibility service (the one that locks the screen), which reads nothing from the screen. Banking apps are left alone by the safe mode.
LOCK SCREEN
the Metro lock screen
A lock screen with your photo, a big clock and what you want to see: the next alarm, notifications per app, weather, next event, music.

Android does not let a launcher replace its lock screen. The Metro one is made ready over it when the screen switches off (it needs the accessibility service), and it also runs as the screen saver while the phone charges.
Try it without locking the phone with “preview”. It can have a photo of its own; without one it uses the photo of Start.
The spot for the fingerprint can be moved or turned off if the sensor is on the side. Everything shown here can be read by anyone who looks at the screen: choose with care.
ACCESSIBILITY
easier to read
Make the launcher fit your eyes and your hands.
Text size from 85 to 130 percent, bold text, one of twenty fonts or a font file of your own.
Reduce motion: screens fade instead of swinging, tiles stop flipping, apps open without an animation. Stronger contrast gives tiles a white frame and makes grey text solid.
TalkBack reads every tile and its notifications. In its actions menu a tile offers unpin, change size, move earlier or later (folders: rename, take apart).
With a keyboard, every tile, row and button takes focus, shows a ring and is pressed with Enter or Space. The pages stay usable at the largest text size.
PRIVACY
keep it safe
A few features keep your things from prying eyes, and keep banks happy.

Safe mode for banking apps (on from the start): while a bank is in front, MetroWin takes away its buttons, bars, banners and the Action Center strip, and puts them back when you leave. Banks refuse to run under overlays.
Lock an app behind your fingerprint or screen lock. The lock is for opening from the launcher (list, tiles, search, voice), not for Android as a whole.
The kid’s corner is a Start with only the apps you choose, for sharing the phone with a child. Leaving it asks for your screen lock.
Live tiles of other apps can show the text of your messages to anyone who sees the screen: they are off until you turn them on, and “hide what is written” keeps the text off the tiles.
BACKUP
backup and sync
Your layout and your settings are worth keeping, and moving to a new phone.
Save them to a file or to a folder, any folder Android can open (also one of Google Drive), by hand or every day, week or month.
Restore asks which parts to put back: Start, settings, look, data. The copies kept are listed, the newest first, and a restore can be undone.
Keep two phones in sync through the same folder: the file is encrypted with a passphrase that only you know and that never goes in the folder.
Pause or hide the work profile and the private space, and save the list of your apps to find them again on a new phone.

Switches on together: the Classic look, the Retro application bar, the original turnstile and the narrow page margin (18 dp, as on Windows Phone). The accent, light or dark, and the tiles stay as they are.
